summary: Sharia is, in the tradition's own usage, the revealed path or law of God: the totality of divine guidance for human life, understood as coming from God rather than from human legislation. It is commonly distinguished from fiqh, the human jurisprudential understanding and elaboration of that guidance, and it is said to govern both worship (ibadat) and social and legal dealings (muamalat). Its sources, its diverse legal schools (madhhabs), and the modern debates over codifying it and relating it to the modern state are matters treated differently by different scholars and left unadjudicated here.
description:
Sharia (from the root sh-r-ʿ; the noun is often glossed as a path to water, and by extension a clear way to be followed) names, in the tradition's self-understanding, the divinely revealed way of life: the guidance God has given for how human beings should live, worship, and deal with one another. The Qur'an uses a cognate in Q 45:18, which in the Sahih International rendering addresses the Prophet, 'Then We put you, [O Muhammad], on an ordained way [shariʿatin] concerning the matter [of religion]; so follow it and do not follow the inclinations of those who do not know.' On this and related texts the tradition builds the understanding of sharia as a God-given path rather than a merely human order.

A distinction commonly drawn by Muslim scholars separates sharia, the revealed law as it is in itself, from fiqh, the human effort to understand and articulate it. On this account sharia is divine and one, while fiqh is the fallible, plural, and revisable jurisprudence of the scholars; the difference is used to explain how the law can be held to be from God even as jurists disagree. Sharia in this broad sense is described as covering two great domains: acts of worship (ibadat), such as the ritual prayer, fasting (see Q 2:183, 'decreed upon you is fasting as it was decreed upon those before you'), almsgiving, and pilgrimage; and social, civil, and legal transactions (muamalat), such as contracts, marriage and family, inheritance, and criminal matters. The classical Sunni account names its sources (usul al-fiqh, the roots of the law), most commonly the Qur'an, the Sunna of the Prophet, the consensus of the scholars (ijmaʿ), and reasoning by analogy (qiyas), with further disputed methods recognized by some jurists and not others.

Out of this activity of interpretation arose the legal schools (madhhabs). In Sunni Islam the four surviving schools, the Hanafi, Maliki, Shafiʿi, and Hanbali, differ in method and in many concrete rulings, and Twelver and other Shiʿi traditions have their own schools; the tradition regards this diversity of the schools as a longstanding feature of the law rather than a defect, and the schools themselves differ on many questions without one being ruled correct here. In the modern period, scholars and states have debated whether and how sharia should be codified into the statutes of a modern nation-state, and what the relation is between a jurists' law developed over centuries and the legislative machinery of the modern state. Wael Hallaq argues that the modern state's codification of law worked a deep transformation of the historical sharia rather than a simple continuation of it; other scholars read the relation differently. These positions are recorded here as attributed scholarly views, not settled by the editor.

This entry presents sharia strictly as the tradition's own concept of a revealed law and a path of religious and social order, described on its own terms (neutrality #6), and not through any external caricature of it. Its internal diversity, the schools, and the classical and modern debates are attributed to those who hold the several positions, and none is adjudicated here.
editorial_notes:
SENSITIVITY CRUX: sharia is a term that carries heavy external political and media connotations. Per neutrality #6 this entry deliberately describes sharia only as the tradition's own concept, the revealed divine law or path (Q 45:18) and a religious-social order, on its own terms, and never as the media caricature; contested points are attributed and not ruled on. The Qur'anic term and its scriptural anchor are treated as the textual basis the tradition itself invokes, not as the editor's proof of any doctrine (neutrality #1, #3).

ATTRIBUTION: the sharia-versus-fiqh distinction (revealed law versus human jurisprudence), the enumeration of the four sources (Qur'an, Sunna, ijmaʿ, qiyas), the diversity of the legal schools, and the classical-versus-modern debate over codification and the modern state are all presented as attributed positions of the scholars who hold them, not as adjudicated fact. Phrasing such as 'in the tradition's self-understanding', 'commonly distinguished', 'the classical Sunni account names', 'Hallaq argues', and 'other scholars read the relation differently' marks the attribution. The internal diversity of the madhhabs is stated and not ranked (neutrality #2, #7).

CONFIDENCE HONESTY: the TERM sharia and its scriptural anchor are open and were read verbatim: Q 45:18 was read line by line at quran.com in two translations (Sahih International, 'Then We put you, [O Muhammad], on an ordained way concerning the matter [of religion]; so follow it', and the Clear Quran, 'Now We have set you on the clear Way of faith'), and the load-bearing word shariʿatin was confirmed in the Arabic; the legal ayah Q 2:183 on fasting was likewise read verbatim (Sahih International, 'decreed upon you is fasting as it was decreed upon those before you'). Those Qur'anic sources are rated high. The distinctive SYSTEM concept, however (the four sources, the schools and their differences, the codification and modern-state debates), rests on modern scholarship, above all Hallaq and Kamali, which was web-verified to exist and be on-topic but not read page by page in this pass and is rated medium. Because the load-bearing systematic content rests on medium sources, this entry honestly tops out at 'reviewed', not 'verified', even though its scriptural anchor is verbatim-confirmed; it is entered as 'draft' pending review.

relations.note: Sharia (the revealed divine law as it is in itself) is commonly distinguished by Muslim scholars from fiqh (the fallible, plural human jurisprudence that seeks to understand and articulate it); the distinction is attributed to the tradition, not adjudicated. Target is a forward reference; fiqh does not yet exist as an entry.
The interpretive elaboration of sharia produced the legal schools (madhhabs), which differ in method and rulings; the diversity is described and not ranked. Target is a forward reference.
Consensus of the scholars (ijmaʿ) is named in the classical Sunni account as one of the sources (usul) of the law. Target (ijma) exists in the dataset.
Reasoning by analogy (qiyas) is named in the classical Sunni account as one of the sources of the law. Target is a forward reference; qiyas does not yet exist as an entry.

Shared question: both sharia and halakha are their tradition's concept of a divinely given law ordering the whole of communal and personal life, worship and social dealings alike, and elaborated by scholars into a body of jurisprudence. Difference: they rest on different revelations, sources, and interpretive institutions, and each is described on its own terms; no ranking or equivalence of the two is asserted (neutrality #10).

Shared question: both sharia and Christian canon law are a tradition's ordered body of religious law governing communal life. Difference: canon law in the Christian traditions is largely the enacted law of ecclesial authority, whereas sharia is understood as revealed divine guidance elaborated by jurists; the shared theme of religious law as social order is noted without ranking either (neutrality #10). Target (canon-law) exists in the dataset.

historical_period.note: The Qur'anic term (Q 45:18) belongs to the period of the Prophet's mission (c. 610-632 CE); sharia as a systematic concept, its sources (usul al-fiqh), and the legal schools were elaborated across the classical centuries, and the debates over codification and the modern state belong to the modern period. No end date is given, as the concept and its debates remain live.

sources.citation: The Qur'an 45:18 (Surat al-Jathiya). Read line by line at quran.com in two translations: Sahih International, 'Then We put you, [O Muhammad], on an ordained way [sharīʿatin] concerning the matter [of religion]; so follow it and do not follow the inclinations of those who do not know'; and The Clear Quran (Mustafa Khattab), 'Now We have set you [O Prophet] on the [clear] Way of faith. So follow it, and do not follow the desires of those who do not know.' The load-bearing cognate sharīʿatin (شريعة) was confirmed in the Arabic. Primary scriptural text and the anchor the tradition invokes for sharia as a God-given way; read verbatim.
